sources.title: Learn Pandas in 30 Minutes - Python Pandas Tutorial

steps.title: Install pandas in your project
steps.instructions: Create a project folder and install pandas in the terminal with pip install pandas (pip3 on Mac/Linux). Alternatively run uv init . and then uv add pandas.

targets.caption: Run pip install pandas in the terminal

explanations.topic: Recommended editors and Jupyter notebooks
Setting up a virtual environment with uv

hints: Open the integrated terminal inside your code editor.
On Windows use pip install pandas; on Mac or Linux use pip3 install pandas.
If pip fails or you want an isolated environment, run uv init . followed by uv add pandas.
common_mistakes: Using pip instead of pip3 on Mac or Linux when Python 3 is mapped to pip3.
Installing pandas globally while the editor uses a separate virtual environment.
Running uv add pandas without first initializing the project with uv init .

steps.title: Import pandas in main.py
steps.instructions: Create main.py in your project folder. Add import pandas as pd at the top of the file.

targets.caption: Add the pandas import at the top of main.py

explanations.topic: Why pandas is commonly aliased as pd

hints: Make sure you are editing a file named main.py in your project folder.
Use Python's import ... as ... syntax to give pandas a short alias.
Type import pandas as pd on line 1 of main.py and save the file.
common_mistakes: Misspelling pandas (for example as panda).
Forgetting to save main.py after typing the import statement.
Selecting the wrong Python interpreter in the editor, causing an unresolved import warning.

steps.title: Load and print CSV in Python
steps.instructions: Download orders.csv from https://github.com/techwithtim/PanadasTutorial into your project folder and create main.py with import pandas as pd, df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv") and print(df). Run python main.py (or uv run main.py) in the terminal to print the DataFrame.

targets.caption: Load orders.csv into df and print it
Check the printed DataFrame dimensions

explanations.topic: DataFrame and Series core Pandas types
CSV file structure with headers and rows

hints: Use Pandas' read_csv function with the CSV filename as a string.
Assign pd.read_csv("orders.csv") to df and pass df to print().
Write df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv") on line 3 and print(df) on line 4, then run uv run .\main.py.
common_mistakes: Placing orders.csv in a different folder than the working directory when running the script.
Writing read_csv without the pd. prefix or forgetting quotes around the filename.

steps.title: Create and save Jupyter notebook
steps.instructions: Open the Command Palette (Cmd+Shift+P), run Create: New Jupyter Notebook, and save it as notebook.ipynb in the project folder. Make sure the Python and Jupyter extensions are installed.

targets.caption: Save the new Jupyter notebook as notebook.ipynb

explanations.topic: Why Jupyter Notebooks suit interactive Pandas analysis

hints: Press Ctrl+Shift+P (or Cmd+Shift+P on macOS) and search for Jupyter.
Choose Create: New Jupyter Notebook and save it as notebook.ipynb in your project folder.
common_mistakes: Saving the notebook with a .py extension instead of .ipynb.
Missing the Microsoft Python extension needed to render and execute notebook cells.

steps.title: Load and print CSV in notebook
steps.instructions: In the first cell of notebook.ipynb, import pandas as pd, load your CSV (e.g. orders.csv) into df with pd.read_csv, and run the cell after selecting a Python kernel. Add a second cell with print(df) and run it.

targets.caption: Load the CSV in the first notebook cell
Print df in the second cell

explanations.topic: Executing individual notebook cells independently

hints: Start by selecting your project's Python kernel when running the first cell.
Put import pandas as pd and df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv") in cell 1, then run it.
Create a new code cell below with + Code, type print(df), and click the play button.
common_mistakes: Running the second cell with print(df) before executing the first cell that defines df.
Selecting a global Python kernel that does not have pandas installed instead of the project environment.
steps.code: import pandas as pd  df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")  print(df)

steps.title: Inspect first and last rows
steps.instructions: In a notebook cell, call df.head() and run it to view the first five rows. Then change it to df.tail() and run the cell to view the last five rows.

targets.caption: Run df.head() and then df.tail() in the cell

explanations.topic: Previewing the top five rows with df.head()
Previewing the bottom five rows with df.tail()

hints: DataFrames have built-in methods to preview the start and end without printing every row.
Call df.head() first, then replace it with df.tail() and run the cell.
common_mistakes: Omitting the parentheses on df.head() or df.tail(), which prints the bound method instead of rows.
Wrapping df.head() inside print() unnecessarily, which loses the formatted HTML table preview.

steps.title: Inspect schema and summary statistics
steps.instructions: Run df.info() in a cell to check column types and non-null counts. Then run df.describe() to get descriptive statistics for the numeric columns.

targets.caption: Inspect schema with df.info() and stats with df.describe()

explanations.topic: Reading column data types and non-null counts from df.info()
Interpreting summary statistics from df.describe()

hints: Use info() to inspect column dtypes and describe() for numerical summaries.
Run df.info() in the cell, inspect the output, then run df.describe().
common_mistakes: Forgetting parentheses on df.info() or df.describe().
Expecting df.describe() to include text columns by default instead of numeric columns only.

steps.title: Inspect column names and index
steps.instructions: Run df.columns in your notebook.ipynb cell to view all column labels. Then run df.index to inspect the DataFrame's row index range.

targets.caption: Run df.columns and then df.index

explanations.topic: Listing column headers with df.columns
Understanding row RangeIndex with df.index

hints: Unlike head() and info(), columns and index are attributes rather than methods.
Run df.columns without parentheses, then run df.index without parentheses.
common_mistakes: Adding parentheses like df.columns() or df.index(), which raises a TypeError because Index objects are not callable.

steps.title: Select single and multiple columns
steps.instructions: Create notebook.ipynb, load your CSV with df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv") and select one column with df["Country"] to see a Series. Then pass a list like df[["Country", "Product"]] to get a new DataFrame.

targets.caption: Pass a list of column names inside double brackets

explanations.topic: Single column returns a pandas Series
Multiple columns return a DataFrame

hints: Check the available column names first with df.columns.
Use single brackets df["col"] for a Series, and double brackets df[["col1", "col2"]] for a DataFrame.
common_mistakes: Passing multiple column names in single brackets instead of wrapping them in a list.
Misspelling a column name or using the wrong capitalization.

steps.title: Index rows with iloc
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb, use df.iloc with a zero-based integer index to retrieve a single row as a Series, then run the cell. Chain a position or column name after df.iloc[row] to access a specific cell value.

targets.caption: Select a row by its integer position

explanations.topic: What iloc stands for (index location)
Accessing individual values from an iloc row

hints: Use square brackets with .iloc rather than parentheses.
Try df.iloc[0] for the first row, then add ["Country"] or ["Shipped"] to pull a single value.
common_mistakes: Writing df.iloc(0) with parentheses instead of square brackets df.iloc[0].
Forgetting that iloc uses zero-based integer positions.

steps.title: Filter rows with boolean conditions
steps.instructions: Filter df with a column comparison inside df[...], then combine two conditions with & or | wrapping each in parentheses. Practice numeric comparisons like >, <= and != on a numeric column.

targets.caption: Wrap each condition in parentheses when combining with & or |

explanations.topic: How boolean filtering works on a DataFrame
Using single & and | operators in pandas

hints: Put the boolean expression inside df[...], like df[df["Category"] == "Electronics"].
When combining two conditions, wrap each in parentheses and use & or | instead of and/or.
common_mistakes: Using Python keywords 'and' or 'or' instead of '&' or '|'.
Forgetting parentheses around each condition when combining filters with & or |.

steps.title: Filter using str and isin methods
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb, filter text columns with .str.startswith() or .str.endswith(), then match rows against a list with .isin([...]) and negate it with ~. Run each cell to see the filtered DataFrame.

targets.caption: Match rows against any value in a list

explanations.topic: Using .str string methods for filtering
Using .isin() and ~ to invert a filter

hints: Access string methods on a Series via .str before calling startswith or endswith.
Pass a list of target values to .isin([...]) and place ~ before the condition to negate it.
common_mistakes: Calling .startswith() directly on a Series without .str.
Passing a single string instead of a list to .isin().
Forgetting that startswith and endswith are case-sensitive.

steps.title: Update cells and columns with loc
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb, use df.loc[condition, column] = value to update matching rows, then transform a whole column with df[col] = df[col].str.upper(). Run the cells and display df to see the changes.

targets.caption: Locate rows by condition and specify the column to update

explanations.topic: How df.loc locates rows by label or condition
Bulk updating multiple matching rows
Transforming an entire column in place

hints: Pass both a row condition and a target column name to df.loc[row_cond, col_name].
Reassign the column back to itself, such as df["Country"] = df["Country"].str.upper(), to persist the change.
common_mistakes: Writing df[cond]["Col"] = val instead of df.loc[cond, "Col"] = val, which mutates a copy instead of df.
Calling .str.upper() without assigning the result back to the DataFrame column.

steps.title: Delete a row by index
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb, drop a row by index with df = df.drop(39) and run the cell, then run df.tail() to verify it was removed.

targets.caption: Drop a row and inspect the tail

explanations.topic: Removing a row by index with df.drop()

hints: How do you remove a row by its index label in pandas?
Use df.drop() with the row index and assign the result back to df.
Write df = df.drop(39) in one cell and df.tail() in the next cell.
common_mistakes: Calling df.drop(39) without assigning back to df or passing inplace=True
Running df.drop(39) a second time after index 39 has already been removed (raises KeyError)

steps.title: Clean nulls and rename columns
steps.instructions: Run df.dropna() to drop missing values (or df.fillna(..., inplace=True)), then rename a column with df.rename(columns={...}, inplace=True) and print df.

targets.caption: Rename a column in place

explanations.topic: Dropping missing values with df.dropna()
Filling missing values and inplace=True
Renaming columns with df.rename()

hints: Which DataFrame methods drop or fill missing (NA) values?
Pass a columns dictionary and inplace=True to df.rename() to modify df directly.
Run df.rename(columns={"OrderID": "Order ID"}, inplace=True) and then df.
common_mistakes: Forgetting inplace=True (or reassigning df) when calling df.rename() or df.fillna()
Assigning the return value of an inplace=True call back to df, which sets df to None

steps.title: Count values in Country column
steps.instructions: Select a categorical column (e.g. df["Country"]) and call .value_counts() to count how many rows have each value.

targets.caption: Count occurrences of each value

explanations.topic: Counting unique column values with value_counts()

hints: How do you count how often each unique value appears in a Series?
Select df["Country"] and chain .value_counts().
Run df["Country"].value_counts() in a new cell.
common_mistakes: Misspelling the column name or using lowercase "country" instead of "Country"
Calling value_counts without parentheses

steps.title: Group by country and sum prices
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb, group the DataFrame by a category column (e.g. "Country"), select a numeric column (e.g. "Price"), and call .sum() to total it per group.

targets.caption: Group rows and sum a column

explanations.topic: Grouping rows and aggregating with groupby()

hints: Which pandas method groups rows by a column before aggregating?
Call df.groupby("Country"), select ["Price"], and chain .sum().
Run df.groupby("Country")["Price"].sum().
common_mistakes: Forgetting to select ["Price"] before calling .sum(), which sums all numeric columns
Using square brackets instead of parentheses for df.groupby("Country")

steps.title: Sort rows by Price descending
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb, sort the DataFrame from highest to lowest with df.sort_values("Price", ascending=False) and run the cell.

targets.caption: Sort rows descending

explanations.topic: Sorting DataFrame rows with sort_values()

hints: How do you sort a DataFrame by a specific column's values?
Use df.sort_values("Price") and pass ascending=False for descending order.
Run df.sort_values("Price", ascending=False) in a new cell.
common_mistakes: Omitting ascending=False, which defaults to ascending (lowest price first)
Writing false in lowercase instead of Python's False

steps.title: Export DataFrame to CSV file
steps.instructions: Save the DataFrame with df.to_csv("new_file.csv", index=False) and run the cell. In the next cell, run pd.read_csv("new_file.csv").shape to confirm the export.

targets.caption: Export the DataFrame to a CSV file
Confirm the exported file's shape

explanations.topic: Saving a DataFrame to CSV with to_csv()

hints: Which DataFrame method exports data to a CSV file?
Call df.to_csv() with the filename and index=False to omit the index column.
Run df.to_csv("new_file.csv", index=False).
common_mistakes: Forgetting index=False, which adds an extra unnamed index column to the CSV
Omitting the .csv file extension in the filename string
